newsitem.title: GERMANY: German jobless surge piles pressure on Kohl to act.
newsitem.headline: German jobless surge piles pressure on Kohl to act.

text.p: A surge in German unemployment to a post-war record has piled the pressure on Chancellor Helmut Kohl to produce results instead of optimistic long-term targets for cutting the jobless rate.

News on Thursday that unemployment had unexpectedly jumped more than half a million to 4.66 million in January dramatically widened the gap between Kohl's goal of halving the rate by the year 2000 and reality.
Politicians from Kohl's centre-right coalition and the opposition quickly blamed each other for the debacle.

"The record unemployment clearly shows Kohl has failed and his misguided economic and financial policies have plunged the country into a dramatic employment crisis," said Oskar Lafontaine, chairman of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

Protests rained down on Kohl after the Federal Labour Office in Nuremberg reported the unemployment rate shot up to 12.2 percent in January from 10.8 percent in December. It was the highest rate recorded in Germany since January 1933.
"Germany with its 4.6 million unemployed is now stuck in the worst job market disaster since the Great Depression," said Ernst Schwanhold, economic policy spokesman for the SPD.
Kohl, often ridiculed for his unemployment goal, was urged to speed up tax and welfare reform to boost investment and job creation, or find himself out of a job.

"We don't need any more fancy words and phrases," said Rudolf Scharping, SPD parliamentary leader. "We need a real turnaround. We need lower labour costs and a genuine tax reform starting in January that gives companies real relief."

But Finance Minister Theo Waigel and other government leaders, while calling the latest data alarming, blamed the unemployment rise on the opposition for blocking his reforms in the upper house of parliament, which the SPD controls.

"The latest data urgently underline the fact that we have to act now," Waigel said. "The tax and social system reforms are now needed more urgently than ever before...Those who block these needed reforms are turning their backs on the jobless."
Waigel said he would press Labour Minister Norbert Bluem to accelerate the timetable for pension system reform.
Bluem said finger-pointing would not accomplish anything. "Anyone who couldn't figure it out before should now know after these alarming figures that we all have to work together," he said.

Analysts said the unexpected jobless spurt would further strain already stretched budgets and raised the odds that Germany would fail to keep its deficit below 3.0 percent of gross domestic product needed to qualify for the European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Ottmar Schreiner, the SPD's job market spokesman, said that even in western Germany the jobless rate had climbed to intolerably high levels, surging above the three million mark to 3.3 million for the first time.
A record 1.4 million were unemployed in the east -- a jobless rate of 19.9 percent.
"The government has seen its Waterloo," said Schreiner. "Their failed policies have given us a very black Thursday."
Despite the drama, commentators were careful not to use the explosive comparison with the mass unemployment of the Weimar Republic which paved the way for Adolf Hitler's Third Reich.
Germany's rich post-war democracy has so little in common with those desperate days that parallels sometimes made in the popular press in the past are seen as overdone.
Even with this reserve, deputies from Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said they were horrified by the figures.
"It is a horribly high number and should start alarms ringing everywhere," said Friedhelm Ost, CDU economic policy spokesman, admitting Kohl's aim of halving unemployment now appeared audacious.
"The economy is so strangled by high costs that it cannot provide enough jobs. Labour has become too expensive."
